label: window._authorChatCapture
after:
The Dohkar’s voice cut across the clearing before mine could form a full sentence. “Explain yourself, Sacrificiant.”

My mouth was free. The gossamer band lay crumpled at the edge of the spiralgrass, and every First Favored present could now read the Weave-Script that flared across my throat in sharp, defensive gold. I stepped closer to the youth, whose aqua skin had gone chalky and whose eyes still looked wrong. The crowd’s attention pressed like a second skin. I felt the weight of it in the small of my back, in the way my breath wanted to hurry and would not.

“I did not guide her wish,” I said. The words came out steadier than my hands felt. “I did not know what she meant to offer until she spoke it.”

A murmur ran through the mated-pair trees. The older guest who had spoken my father’s name looked at me as though the sound still lived in his mouth. The Dohkar’s hands remained raised in the warding sign, though the ritual was already broken. Every gaze read the misalignment the same way: the supervisor had left her place.

I tried again. “The wish twisted before I moved. I tore the band because the rite was already compromised, not to claim anything for myself.”

Julian had not shifted from the far side of the clearing. I remembered the way he once knelt in the Thornwild undergrowth, coaxing a trapped fox free with the same careful stillness he carried now, refusing to hurry even when the animal’s teeth found his wrist. That memory surfaced without permission, the way it always did when the air grew thin. My pulse answered it before I could steady the rest of me.

The Dohkar cleared his throat. His Weave-Script had gone the flat grey of withheld judgment. “You stepped out of your seal. You spoke while the rite still held. The youth’s sacrifice is spent, and the only question left is whether your interference twisted what Fate accepted.”

The youth’s fingers tightened on her tunic hem. She looked at me once, small and frightened, then away. The Dohkar’s thumb traced a circle on his palm. The crowd shifted their weight with him. Every First Favored present leaned forward for the answer that would decide whether the qualification I had come to earn still existed.

I had no answer that would not cost something I was not yet willing to name.

label: window._authorChatCapture
after:
The moss beneath my feet cushioned the impact of every step, its damp green scent rising in the warmth of the afternoon. I pressed my palm against the moss-covered stone at the edge of the clearing, its surface cool and uneven under my fingers. The Dohkar’s words still rang in my ears—*Explain yourself, Sacrificiant.*—and the accusation pressed against my ribs until each breath came shorter. The youth’s sacrifice had twisted, the bond-thread frayed, and the Alignment Circle would not wait forever.

A murmur rippled through the assembled First Favored, their gossamer tunics catching the light in shifting patches of gold and green. Their Weave-Script flickered in soft golds and violets, each color spelling out the emotions they refused to name aloud. I caught snippets of their whispers: *"misaligned supervisor,betrayed the rite,the bond will fail."* The words cut, but none of them looked at me directly. Not yet.

Then came the rustle of fabric, the snap of a twig. I turned just in time to see a figure emerge from the trees—a Wilder, his aqua skin dull under the sun, his movements too deliberate, too controlled. He wore the quiet confidence of someone who had spent years hiding in plain sight. His gaze locked onto mine, and for a single breath, the space between us narrowed until nothing else held.

The Dohkar’s voice cut through the murmurs again. *"You stand there in silence while the contract unravels. Explain yourself before the Circle makes the decision for you."*

I exhaled through the gossamer band still curled in my fist. A thrush called once from the canopy, the note hanging sharp in the air. She stepped forward and said hello, the word leaving her as though the air itself resisted its passage. The words I needed to say would cost me everything.

The moss beneath my feet cushioned the impact of every step, its damp green scent rising in the warmth of the afternoon. I pressed my palm against the moss-covered stone at the edge of the clearing, its surface cool and uneven under my fingers. The Dohkar’s words still rang in my ears—*Explain yourself, Sacrificiant.*—and the accusation pressed against my ribs until each breath came shorter. The youth’s sacrifice had twisted, the bond-thread frayed, and the Alignment Circle would not wait forever.

A murmur rippled through the assembled First Favored, their gossamer tunics catching the light in shifting patches of gold and green. Their Weave-Script flickered in soft golds and violets, each color spelling out the emotions they refused to name aloud. I caught snippets of their whispers: *"misaligned supervisor, betrayed the rite, the bond will fail."* The words cut, but none of them looked at me directly. Not yet.

Then came the rustle of fabric, the snap of a twig. I turned just in time to see a figure emerge from the trees—a Wilder, his aqua skin dull under the sun, his movements too deliberate, too controlled. He wore the quiet confidence of someone who had spent years hiding in plain sight. His gaze locked onto mine, and for a single breath, the space between us narrowed until nothing else held.

The Dohkar’s voice cut through the murmurs again. *"You stand there in silence while the contract unravels. Explain yourself before the Circle makes the decision for you."*

I exhaled through the gossamer band still curled in my fist. A thrush called once from the canopy, the note hanging sharp in the air. She stepped forward and said hello, the word leaving her as though the air itself resisted its passage. In that moment, the way her laughter burst forth unexpectedly made it feel like a sudden spring rain, and I leaned slightly closer, drawn in by the depth of feeling in her expressive face and the dark auburn waves of her hair that danced around her shoulders. The words I needed to say would cost me everything.
after:
The moss-covered stone in the sunlit clearing held the youth’s discarded offering, the moss darkening beneath it as the light pulled away. I wanted the Dohkar to accept my words and end the scrutiny before the youth’s sacrifice hardened into something worse. The Dohkar wanted proof I had not broken the seal for my own gain.

“Explain yourself, Sacrificiant,” he said again, voice low and edged. “The wish twisted toward you. Tell us why, or the contract you came to earn dies here.”

My fingers tightened on the hem of my cloak. I wanted to shield the youth from the crowd’s gaze and still claim the qualification I had earned through months of study. The Dohkar’s stare pressed for an answer that would either clear me or condemn me outright.

Julian’s gaze lingered on me from the far side of the clearing, making the air between us feel thinner. He stepped forward once, the movement small but enough to draw every eye. “She tore the band after the twist began,” he said. “I saw it. The question now is who placed the interference before any of us spoke.”

The Dohkar turned on him. “You defend the one who left her place?”

My heel bounced once against the moss before I stilled it. A hidden thread of the sigil pulsed against my palm, small and wrong, carrying someone else’s mark. The youth’s eyes widened, a shiver passing through her frame before she could stop it. The Dohkar waited for my answer while the crowd’s Weave-Script flared with suspicion.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds—or maybe arcing up? Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present…
